entries.1:1: Paul introduces himself as someone chosen by God to represent Jesus, and he mentions a fellow believer named Sosthenes standing with him. This shows the letter comes from a real person with God-given authority, not just his own opinion.
entries.1:2: The letter is addressed to ordinary believers in Corinth who have been set apart for God through Jesus, along with everyone everywhere who calls on Jesus. It reminds the reader that being part of God's people is about belonging to Jesus, not about being in a special place.
entries.1:3: Paul wishes his readers kindness and peace from God and Jesus. It's a warm blessing that reminds the reader that real peace comes from God, not from circumstances.
entries.1:4: Paul regularly thanks God for the Corinthian believers because God has been generous to them through Jesus. It encourages the reader to notice and be grateful for what God has done in other people's lives.
entries.1:5: Because of Jesus, these believers have been enriched in what they say and in what they understand. It means God gives real gifts to ordinary people, including the ability to speak and to know things deeply.
entries.1:6: The message about Jesus had been firmly confirmed among them by what they experienced. It reminds the reader that the good news about Jesus is not just a story but something that proves true in real lives.
entries.1:7: They have every spiritual gift and are waiting with hope for Jesus to return. It tells the reader that waiting for Jesus is meant to be filled with hope, not fear, because God has already given them what they need.
entries.1:8: Jesus himself will keep them strong to the end so they can stand blameless when he comes. It reassures the reader that staying faithful isn't something they must do alone; God does the keeping.
entries.1:9: God can be trusted, and he is the one who brought them into a relationship with his Son. It means the reader's security rests on God's reliability, not on their own performance.
entries.1:10: Paul urges the believers to stop taking sides and to be united in what they say and think. It challenges the reader to work for unity with other believers rather than letting disagreements split them apart.
entries.1:11: Paul has heard from Chloe's household that there are arguments and splits in the church. It shows that even early churches had conflict, and that honest reports of problems are worth paying attention to.
entries.1:12: People were picking favorite leaders and saying they belonged to Paul, Apollos, Peter, or even Christ. It warns the reader against turning Christian leaders into team mascots and dividing over who is best.
entries.1:13: Paul asks pointed questions to show how absurd these divisions are, since Christ is not divided and Paul was not the one crucified for them. It reminds the reader that their identity and salvation come from Jesus alone, not from any human leader.
entries.1:14: Paul is relieved he only baptized a couple of people there. It shows he wanted to avoid any confusion about whose name people were baptized into.
entries.1:15: He didn't want anyone claiming they were baptized into his own name. It's a reminder that baptism is about belonging to Jesus, not about loyalty to a particular pastor or leader.
entries.1:16: Paul remembers baptizing one more household but isn't sure about anyone else. It shows he's being honest and careful about the details rather than exaggerating his role.
entries.1:17: Paul says his main job from Christ is to preach the good news, not to run a baptism program, and to do it plainly so the cross isn't overshadowed by clever talk. It reminds the reader that the message about Jesus is powerful on its own and doesn't need fancy presentation.
entries.1:18: The message about the cross looks like nonsense to people headed for ruin, but to those being saved it is God's power. It tells the reader that what seems weak or foolish to the world can actually be the strongest thing of all.
entries.1:19: God says he will frustrate the wisdom of the wise and cancel the plans of the clever. It means human cleverness can't outsmart God, so the reader shouldn't put ultimate trust in being smart.
entries.1:20: Paul asks where all the wise, scholarly, and debate-loving people of the world have gotten to, since God has shown worldly wisdom to be foolish. It challenges the reader not to be impressed by intellectual status when it comes to knowing God.
entries.1:21: The world with all its wisdom failed to know God, so God chose to save people through the supposedly foolish act of preaching to those who believe. It means God's way of reaching people is simple and available to everyone, not just the brilliant.
entries.1:22: Jewish people wanted miraculous signs and Greek people wanted philosophical arguments. It shows that people often demand God prove himself on their own terms.
entries.1:23: Paul preached a crucified Messiah, which offended the Jews and looked like nonsense to the Greeks. It reminds the reader that the cross will always be unpopular with some people, and that's okay.
entries.1:24: But for those God has called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is God's power and wisdom. It means the very thing people reject is exactly what saves those who believe.
entries.1:25: What looks like foolishness or weakness in God is still far wiser and stronger than anything humans have. It encourages the reader to trust God's ways even when they don't make sense to them.
entries.1:26: Paul points out that not many of the Corinthian believers were impressive by worldly standards of wisdom, power, or status. It reminds the reader that God often chooses ordinary people, so no one needs to feel disqualified.
entries.1:27: God deliberately chose the foolish and weak things of the world to shame the wise and strong. It means God's choices often turn human rankings upside down, giving hope to those the world overlooks.
entries.1:28: God chose the lowly, despised, and insignificant things to bring down the things that seem important. It reassures the reader that being overlooked by the world doesn't mean being overlooked by God.
entries.1:29: The point is that no human being can boast in God's presence. It means salvation and calling are God's doing, so the reader has nothing to brag about and no reason for pride.
entries.1:30: God is the one who placed believers in Christ, who became their wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption. It means everything the reader needs to be right with God is found in Jesus, not in themselves.
entries.1:31: As Scripture says, anyone who wants to boast should boast about the Lord. It encourages the reader to make God the thing they're proud of, rather than themselves.
entries.2:1: Paul reminds the Corinthians that when he first came to them he didn't use fancy speeches or impressive human wisdom to present God's message. It means the messenger doesn't need to be clever or polished for the message to matter.
entries.2:2: Paul deliberately decided that the one thing he would focus on among them was Jesus Christ and his death on the cross. For the reader, it shows that the cross, not human cleverness, is the heart of the Christian message.
entries.2:3: Paul says he came to them feeling weak, afraid, and unsure of himself. This shows that God can work through people who feel inadequate, so the reader doesn't need to feel strong or confident to be useful.
entries.2:4: Paul's preaching didn't rely on clever, persuasive words but on the Spirit's power making the message clear. It means the effect of the message comes from God, not from the speaker's skill.
entries.2:5: Paul wanted their faith to rest on God's power rather than on human wisdom. For the reader, it means your trust should be grounded in what God has done, not in how convincing a person sounds.
entries.2:6: Paul does speak wisdom, but it's a wisdom for the mature, and it's not the kind of wisdom this world or its powerful leaders value, since those things pass away. It means there is real depth in the faith, but it's different from worldly cleverness.
entries.2:7: Paul says they proclaim God's hidden wisdom, which God planned long before the world began, for our benefit and glory. It means God's plan for us is ancient and intentional, not an afterthought.
entries.2:8: None of the world's rulers understood this wisdom, because if they had, they wouldn't have crucified the Lord of glory. It shows that human power and insight can completely miss what God is doing.
entries.2:9: Paul quotes Scripture to say that no eye, ear, or human heart has imagined what God has prepared for those who love him. It means God's good plans for his people are beyond anything we can picture.
entries.2:10: God has revealed these things to us by his Spirit, and the Spirit searches even the deep things of God. It means we can know God's plans not by our own cleverness but because his Spirit shows us.
entries.2:11: Just as only a person's own spirit knows what's inside that person, only God's Spirit knows the things of God. It means understanding God requires his Spirit, not just human reasoning.
entries.2:12: Paul says believers have received God's Spirit, not the spirit of the world, so that we can know what God has freely given us. It means the Spirit helps us understand and appreciate God's gifts.
entries.2:13: Paul says they teach these things not in human wisdom's words but in words taught by the Spirit, explaining spiritual things to spiritual people. It means the message is shaped by God's Spirit rather than by human eloquence.
entries.2:14: A person without the Spirit can't accept the things of God; they seem foolish to him, and he can't understand them because they're understood only through the Spirit. It means spiritual truth requires the Spirit to grasp it.
entries.2:15: The person with the Spirit can evaluate all things, yet is not rightly judged by anyone without the Spirit. It means Spirit-led people have a capacity to discern that others can't assess from the outside.
entries.2:16: No one can know the Lord's mind well enough to instruct him, yet Paul says believers have the mind of Christ. It means we don't stand over God as his teachers; instead, through Christ, we come to share his way of thinking.
entries.3:1: Paul couldn't teach the Corinthians deep truths yet because they were still acting like spiritual beginners. It means we should accept that growth takes time and not be discouraged if we're not mature yet.
entries.3:2: Paul gave them simple teaching, like milk for babies, because they weren't ready for solid food. It reminds us that God feeds us what we can handle at each stage of our growth.
entries.3:3: Their jealousy and arguing showed they were still ruled by selfish human nature rather than God's Spirit. It challenges us to look at how we treat each other as a sign of our real spiritual state.
entries.3:4: Choosing sides around favorite leaders was just ordinary human behavior, not spiritual maturity. It warns us against making heroes out of church leaders and dividing over them.
entries.3:5: Paul and Apollos were only servants who delivered God's message; they weren't the point. It means we should honor leaders without treating them as more than they are.
entries.3:6: Paul started the work and Apollos continued it, but only God made anything actually grow. It reminds us that our efforts matter, but God is the one who brings the results.
entries.3:7: The people who plant and water aren't the important ones; God, who makes things grow, is. It keeps us humble about our role and grateful to God for any growth.
entries.3:8: Those who plant and those who water share one purpose, and each will be rewarded for their own work. It means our part matters, and God will fairly reward each person's effort.
entries.3:9: Paul and the others work alongside God, and the Corinthians themselves are the field and building God is growing. It means we belong to God and are part of what he is building.
entries.3:10: Paul laid the foundation like a skilled builder, and others build on it, but each person must be careful how they build. It means we should think seriously about what we contribute to God's work.
entries.3:11: Jesus Christ is the only foundation anyone can build on. It means everything we do should be built on him, not on anything else.
entries.3:12: People can build with valuable materials or with cheap, flammable ones on that foundation. It means the quality of what we do for God matters, not just the fact that we do something.
entries.3:13: A day is coming when fire will test everyone's work and show what it was really made of. It means we should live and serve with lasting quality in mind, not just appearances.
entries.3:14: If what a person built survives the test, they will receive a reward. It encourages us that faithful work for God is never wasted.
entries.3:15: If a person's work burns up, they lose the reward but are still saved, like someone escaping through fire. It means poor work costs us, but God's grace still saves the person.
entries.3:16: The church itself is God's holy temple, and God's Spirit lives among his people. It means we should treat the church and each other with real respect.
entries.3:17: Anyone who destroys God's temple will face God's judgment, because his temple is holy and that temple is his people. It warns us to take seriously how we treat the church.
entries.3:18: Don't fool yourself; if you think you're wise by the world's standards, you need to become 'foolish' to be truly wise. It means we should humbly let go of worldly cleverness and learn from God.
entries.3:19: What the world calls wisdom looks like foolishness to God, and he catches the clever in their own schemes. It means we shouldn't be impressed by worldly intelligence or rely on it.
entries.3:20: The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise and sees that they amount to nothing. It reminds us that human reasoning apart from God is empty.
entries.3:21: No one should boast about human leaders, because everything belongs to you in Christ. It means we don't need to compete over leaders since God has given us everything in him.
entries.3:22: Even leaders, life, death, the present, and the future all belong to you as God's gift. It means nothing in life or death can ultimately work against those who belong to Christ.
entries.3:23: You belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God. It means our identity and security rest in Christ, who is fully God's.
entries.4:1: Paul says he and his coworkers should be seen simply as servants of Christ who have been trusted with God's hidden truths. Readers should think of church leaders as stewards, not celebrities.
entries.4:2: A servant who is trusted with something must prove faithful and reliable. The reader should aim to be trustworthy with whatever God has entrusted to them.
entries.4:3: Paul says it matters very little to him whether people judge him, and he does not even judge himself. Readers should not live for other people's approval or their own self-assessment.
entries.4:4: Paul's conscience is clear, but that alone does not prove he is right, because the Lord is the one who judges him. Readers should remember that a clear conscience is not the same as being declared right by God.
entries.4:5: So don't pass judgment before the Lord returns, because he will bring hidden motives and intentions into the light. Readers should leave final judgment to God and wait for his timing.
entries.4:6: Paul uses himself and Apollos as examples so the Corinthians will learn not to go beyond what Scripture says or boast against one another. Readers should let Scripture set the limits and avoid pride toward fellow believers.
entries.4:7: Paul asks what makes anyone different and points out that everything we have was received as a gift. Readers should not boast as if they achieved anything on their own.
entries.4:8: Paul speaks with irony, saying the Corinthians act as if they are already full, rich, and ruling as kings without him. Readers should beware of spiritual pride that thinks it has already arrived.
entries.4:9: Paul pictures the apostles as displayed last, like people condemned to die, put on show before the world, angels, and people. Readers should see that following Christ can mean being publicly humbled.
entries.4:10: Paul contrasts the apostles, who look foolish, weak, and shamed for Christ, with the Corinthians, who see themselves as wise, strong, and honored. Readers should not measure spiritual worth by worldly status.
entries.4:11: Paul lists real hardships: hunger, thirst, lack of clothing, beatings, and no settled home. Readers should recognize the cost many servants of Christ have paid.
entries.4:12: Paul and his team do hard manual work and respond to insults with blessings and to mistreatment with patience. Readers should answer hostility with kindness rather than retaliation.
entries.4:13: When people slander them, they answer gently, and Paul says they are treated like the world's garbage and refuse. Readers should expect that faithful service may bring contempt, and respond with grace.
entries.4:14: Paul says he writes these things not to shame them but to warn them as his dear children. Readers should receive correction as loving guidance, not as humiliation.
entries.4:15: Even if they had countless teachers, they have only one spiritual father, because Paul brought them to faith through the gospel. Readers should honor those who first led them to Christ.
entries.4:16: Paul urges the Corinthians to imitate his example. Readers should look for mature believers whose lives are worth copying.
entries.4:17: Paul is sending Timothy, his dear and faithful child in the Lord, to remind them of Paul's ways in Christ, which he teaches everywhere. Readers should value faithful messengers who pass on consistent teaching.
entries.4:18: Some in Corinth are arrogant, assuming Paul will not actually come to them. Readers should not mistake delay for absence or assume they are beyond accountability.
entries.4:19: Paul plans to come soon, if the Lord allows, and he will test not the proud people's talk but their power. Readers should value real spiritual power over impressive words.
entries.4:20: God's kingdom is not about talk but about power. Readers should look for evidence of God's real work, not just fine speech.
entries.4:21: Paul asks whether they want him to come with discipline or with love and a gentle spirit. Readers should consider how their attitude shapes the way they are corrected.
entries.5:1: Paul reports that a man in the church is sleeping with his father's wife, a sin so shocking that even non-believers don't do it. This means the reader should take sexual sin seriously, even when it happens inside the church.
entries.5:2: Instead of being grieved over this sin, the church is proud of itself and has done nothing about it. The reader is warned that arrogance can blind a church to serious wrong.
entries.5:3: Paul says that even though he is far away physically, he has already made a judgment about this man as if he were present. This means leaders can and should address serious sin even from a distance.
entries.5:4: Paul tells the church to gather in the name and power of Jesus, with his own spirit joined to them, to act on this matter. The reader learns that church discipline should be done prayerfully and under Jesus' authority.
entries.5:5: Paul hands the man over to Satan so his sinful flesh may be destroyed, with the hope that his spirit will be saved on the day Jesus returns. This means the purpose of such severe action is restoration, not revenge.
entries.5:6: Paul says their boasting is not good, because a little yeast works through the whole batch of dough. The reader should see that tolerating sin can spread and affect the whole church.
entries.5:7: Paul tells them to remove the old yeast so they can be a fresh batch, since Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. This means the reader should live free from old sinful patterns because Jesus gave himself for us.
entries.5:8: Paul says to celebrate the feast not with the old yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. The reader is called to honest, sincere living rather than hidden sin.
entries.5:9: Paul reminds them that in an earlier letter he told them not to associate with people who live by sexual sin. This means the reader should take seriously the company they keep and the influence it has.
entries.5:10: Paul clarifies he did not mean avoiding all sinful non-believers, since that would require leaving the world entirely. The reader is not called to isolate from the world but to live wisely within it.
entries.5:11: Paul means that if someone claims to be a believer but lives in sexual sin, greed, insults, drunkenness, or cheating, you should not keep close company or share meals with them. This means the reader should not treat unrepentant sin in a fellow believer as normal.
entries.5:12: Paul says it is not his job to judge outsiders, but it is the church's responsibility to judge those inside the church. The reader should focus on accountability within the church rather than condemning the world.
entries.5:13: Paul says God will judge those outside, and the church should remove the wicked person from among them. This means the reader should trust God with outsiders and take seriously the need to keep the church community pure.
entries.6:1: Christians were taking their disagreements to secular courts instead of letting fellow believers settle them. The point for the reader is to handle conflicts within the church family rather than airing them before outsiders.
entries.6:2: Believers will one day share in judging the world, so they should be able to handle small disputes now. The reader is reminded that everyday disagreements are far below their calling.
entries.6:3: If believers will even judge angels, ordinary matters of daily life should be easy for them to settle. The reader should not think any everyday dispute is too hard for the church to handle.
entries.6:4: Paul asks why they hand their daily-life cases to judges outside the church who have no standing among believers. The reader is urged to look for wise resolution inside the church instead.
entries.6:5: Paul says this to make them feel ashamed that no wise person among them could settle a dispute between brothers. The reader is challenged to value the wisdom already present in the church.
entries.6:6: Instead of settling things among themselves, believers were dragging each other into court before unbelievers. The reader is warned against letting disputes become public lawsuits.
entries.6:7: Going to court against each other at all is already a loss for believers; better to accept being wronged or cheated. The reader is encouraged to value peace over winning.
entries.6:8: Rather than accepting loss, they were the ones doing wrong and cheating their own brothers. The reader is warned against harming fellow believers while claiming to be in the right.
entries.6:9: Paul reminds them that people who live in wrongdoing will not share in God's kingdom, and lists serious sins as examples. The reader is warned not to be deceived about how they live.
entries.6:10: He continues the list, naming thieves, drunkards, slanderers, and swindlers as excluded from God's kingdom. The reader is reminded that such habits cut a person off from God's rule.
entries.6:11: Some of them had lived that way, but they were washed, made holy, and put right with God through Jesus and the Spirit. The reader is encouraged that a changed life is genuinely possible.
entries.6:12: Paul says he is free to do many things, but not everything is helpful, and he refuses to be controlled by anything. The reader is challenged to use freedom without becoming enslaved to it.
entries.6:13: Food and stomach are temporary things that will pass, but the body is meant for the Lord and the Lord for the body. The reader is reminded that their body has a higher purpose than mere appetite.
entries.6:14: God raised Jesus from the dead and will raise believers too by his power. The reader is given hope that their body matters and will be raised.
entries.6:15: Believers' bodies are part of Christ himself, so joining them to a prostitute is unthinkable. The reader is reminded that their body is tied to Christ, not just to themselves.
entries.6:16: Paul cites Scripture that two people who join sexually become one flesh, so such a union is real and binding. The reader is warned that sexual choices create real bonds, not casual ones.
entries.6:17: Whoever is united to the Lord becomes one spirit with him. The reader is encouraged that closeness with Christ shapes who they are.
entries.6:18: Paul urges them to flee sexual sin, noting that it uniquely harms a person's own body. The reader is advised to avoid it rather than flirt with it.
entries.6:19: The body is a dwelling place for the Holy Spirit given by God, so believers do not own themselves. The reader is reminded that their body belongs to God and is his home.
entries.6:20: God paid a price to buy them, so they should honor him with their bodies. The reader is called to live in a way that reflects who they now belong to.
entries.7:1: Paul is answering a question the church asked him, and he agrees that staying single can be a good thing. For the reader, this means singleness is a valid and honorable choice, not a lesser life.
entries.7:2: Because sexual temptation is real, Paul says each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. For the reader, marriage is the proper setting for sexual intimacy and a safeguard against temptation.
entries.7:3: Husbands and wives owe each other sexual intimacy as part of their marriage commitment. For the reader, this is a mutual responsibility, not something one spouse can withhold from the other.
entries.7:4: In marriage, each spouse's body belongs to the other, so neither has sole say over it. For the reader, this means intimacy in marriage is a shared gift, not a private possession.
entries.7:5: Couples may pause intimacy only by mutual agreement and for a limited time, such as for prayer, then resume so temptation doesn't win. For the reader, this calls for honest agreement rather than one-sided decisions about intimacy.
entries.7:6: Paul makes clear this advice about pausing intimacy is his own pastoral suggestion, not a direct command from Jesus. For the reader, this shows some guidance in Scripture is wise counsel rather than strict law.
entries.7:7: Paul wishes everyone could be single like him, but he recognizes God gives different gifts to different people. For the reader, whether married or single, your situation is a gift from God, not a mistake.
entries.7:8: Paul tells unmarried people and widows that staying single, as he does, is a good option. For the reader, being single or widowed is not a problem to fix but a legitimate way to live.
entries.7:9: If someone lacks self-control, Paul says it's better to marry than to be consumed by desire. For the reader, marriage is the right choice for those who struggle with sexual temptation.
entries.7:10: Here Paul passes on Jesus' own teaching: a wife should not leave her husband. For the reader, this is not just Paul's opinion but a command from the Lord about keeping marriage together.
entries.7:11: If a wife does separate, she should stay unmarried or reconcile with her husband, and the same applies to husbands. For the reader, separation should never be treated lightly or as a quick escape from marriage.
entries.7:12: Paul gives his own counsel, not a direct word from Jesus, about Christians married to non-Christians: if the non-Christian wants to stay, don't leave. For the reader, faith differences alone are not a reason to walk out of a marriage.
entries.7:13: A Christian woman with a non-Christian husband who wants to stay should not leave him either. For the reader, the same principle applies to both spouses: stay unless the unbelieving partner chooses to go.
entries.7:14: Paul says the unbelieving spouse and the children are set apart through the believing partner's faith. For the reader, your faith in a mixed home is not wasted; it brings a special blessing to your family.
entries.7:15: If the non-Christian partner insists on leaving, let them go; God calls us to live in peace, not to force a marriage. For the reader, you are not bound to keep someone who refuses to stay.
entries.7:16: No one can be sure whether their faithful presence will lead their spouse to faith. For the reader, this is a reason to stay and keep trusting God rather than give up too soon.
entries.7:17: Paul's rule for all churches is that people should live out their calling in the situation God placed them in. For the reader, you don't need to change your circumstances to serve God faithfully where you are.
entries.7:18: Whether a person was circumcised or not before becoming a Christian doesn't matter now, so no change is needed. For the reader, outward religious status from your past doesn't affect your standing with God.
entries.7:19: Circumcision or uncircumcision counts for nothing; what matters is obeying God's commands. For the reader, God cares about your obedience, not your religious background or rituals.
entries.7:20: Each person should remain in the life situation God assigned them when they were called. For the reader, contentment in your current place is itself a way of honoring God.
entries.7:21: If you were a slave when you became a Christian, don't be troubled by it, but take freedom if the opportunity comes. For the reader, your circumstances don't limit God's work in you, and it's fine to improve your situation.
entries.7:22: A slave who belongs to the Lord is truly free, and a free person who belongs to the Lord is truly a servant. For the reader, your true identity and freedom come from Christ, not your social status.
entries.7:23: Christ paid a price to buy you, so don't let people own you. For the reader, your loyalty belongs to Jesus first, not to any human master or system.
entries.7:24: Paul repeats: stay in the condition God placed you in when you were called. For the reader, serve God right where you are rather than waiting for perfect circumstances.
entries.7:25: About unmarried women, Paul has no direct command from Jesus but offers his trustworthy opinion as one shown mercy. For the reader, this is wise counsel from a faithful leader, not a strict law.
entries.7:26: Because of the present hardships, Paul thinks it's good for people to stay as they are. For the reader, in difficult times, keeping life simple and steady can be wise.
entries.7:27: If you're married, don't seek to be free; if you're not married, don't rush to marry. For the reader, don't be restless about your marital status; be content where you are.
entries.7:28: Marrying is not a sin for anyone, though married people will face extra troubles in life. For the reader, marriage is good but comes with real challenges, so choose it with open eyes.
entries.7:29: Paul says time is short, so married people should hold their marriages loosely. For the reader, don't let even good things like marriage crowd out your focus on God's kingdom.
entries.7:30: Those who are sad or happy or buying things should not be consumed by these feelings or possessions. For the reader, let joy and sorrow and money be held lightly because this life is passing.
entries.7:31: Don't be absorbed in the world's goods, because the world as it is will soon pass away. For the reader, enjoy what God gives without letting it become your whole life.
entries.7:32: Paul wants you free from worries; an unmarried man can focus on pleasing the Lord. For the reader, singleness offers freedom to devote more attention to God's work.
entries.7:33: A married man has to think about worldly matters and how to please his wife. For the reader, marriage rightly brings divided attention, and that's a normal part of it.
entries.7:34: An unmarried woman can focus on being holy in body and spirit, while a married woman thinks about pleasing her husband. For the reader, both paths have value, but each carries different concerns.
entries.7:35: Paul says all this for your benefit, not to restrict you, so you can serve the Lord without distraction. For the reader, his advice aims at your good and freedom, not to burden you.
entries.7:36: If a man feels he's treating his fiancée unfairly, especially as she gets older, he should go ahead and marry her; it's no sin. For the reader, marriage is a perfectly good and honorable choice.
entries.7:37: A man who is settled in his decision and controls his desires does well to stay unmarried. For the reader, staying single by deliberate choice, not pressure, is also honorable.
entries.7:38: So the man who marries does well, and the one who stays unmarried does better. For the reader, both choices are good, and neither should be looked down on.
entries.7:39: A wife is bound to her husband while he lives, but if he dies she is free to remarry, though only to a Christian. For the reader, widows may remarry, and faith should guide that choice.
entries.7:40: In Paul's opinion, a widow will be happier staying unmarried, and he believes he has the Spirit of God in saying this. For the reader, this is Spirit-guided wisdom, not a command, so weigh it prayerfully.
entries.8:1: Knowing the right facts can make a person proud, but love is what actually builds people up. What matters for you is that your knowledge should be used to help others, not to make yourself look important.
entries.8:2: If you think you have everything figured out, you really don't yet know as much as you should. It's a warning to stay humble about what you know.
entries.8:3: The person who truly loves God is known by God. What counts is a real relationship with God, not just being smart about him.
entries.8:4: Since an idol is just a piece of material and there is only one real God, food sacrificed to idols is not actually contaminated. So eating it isn't wrong in itself.
entries.8:5: People may call many things gods or lords, whether in heaven or on earth. The world around us is full of things people treat as gods.
entries.8:6: For us there is one God, the Father, who made everything and for whom we live, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom everything was made and through whom we live. Our whole life is meant to be centered on God and Jesus.
entries.8:7: Not everyone understands that idols are nothing; some people were so used to idol worship that eating such food still bothers their conscience. You should be patient with people whose faith is still weak.
entries.8:8: God doesn't accept or reject us based on what we eat; food doesn't make us better or worse. So don't treat this as a test of who is a good Christian.
entries.8:9: Be careful that your freedom doesn't become a trap for someone whose faith is weak. Your rights should not trip up others.
entries.8:10: If a weaker believer sees you, who know better, eating in an idol's temple, they may be encouraged to do something their conscience can't handle. Your example can lead someone the wrong way.
entries.8:11: Your knowledge could end up ruining a brother or sister for whom Christ died. That's a serious cost for exercising your freedom.
entries.8:12: When you hurt fellow believers and wound their weak conscience, you are sinning against Christ himself. How you treat other believers matters to Jesus.
entries.8:13: Paul says he would give up eating meat permanently rather than cause a brother to stumble. Love for others should shape what you are willing to give up.
entries.9:1: Paul is defending his authority by pointing out that he is free, has seen the risen Jesus, and that the Corinthian believers themselves are proof of his work. For the reader, it means a person's changed life can be real evidence that someone's ministry is genuine.
entries.9:2: Paul says that even if others doubt his apostleship, the Corinthians should not, because their own faith is the living proof of it. For the reader, it means the fruit of someone's work speaks louder than others' opinions.
entries.9:3: Paul is stating that this is his defense against those who are criticizing him. For the reader, it means it is fair to calmly explain yourself when you are being judged unfairly.
entries.9:4: Paul asks whether he and his coworkers have the right to be supported with food and drink. For the reader, it means people who serve others full-time can rightly expect basic support.
entries.9:5: Paul points out that other apostles, including Peter, travel with their wives and are supported, so he should have the same right. For the reader, it means it is reasonable for those who serve God to have normal family life and support.
entries.9:6: Paul asks whether he and Barnabas alone are expected to work for a living while doing ministry. For the reader, it means it is not wrong for ministers to receive help rather than always supporting themselves.
entries.9:7: Paul uses everyday examples of soldiers, farmers, and shepherds to show that workers normally benefit from their labor. For the reader, it means it is fair and normal for those who do the work to share in the results.
entries.9:8: Paul says this is not just his own human opinion, because God's law teaches the same principle. For the reader, it means God's word confirms what common sense already suggests about fair treatment of workers.
entries.9:9: Paul quotes a law about not muzzling an ox as it grinds grain, then asks whether God cares only about oxen. For the reader, it means God's commands often carry a wider principle about fairness that applies to people too.
entries.9:10: Paul explains that this law was written with people in mind, since workers who plow and thresh should do so with hope of sharing the harvest. For the reader, it means those who work should be able to expect a fair share of what they produce.
entries.9:11: Paul says that since he has given the Corinthians spiritual blessings, it is a small thing for them to share material support with him. For the reader, it means it is reasonable to support those who have invested in your spiritual growth.
entries.9:12: Paul says that if others have a right to support from the Corinthians, he has even more, yet he chose not to use that right so nothing would hinder the gospel. For the reader, it means sometimes giving up your rights is worth it to keep the message clear.
entries.9:13: Paul points out that temple workers and altar servants receive their living from the offerings brought to the temple. For the reader, it means it is an old and normal pattern that those who serve at a place of worship are supported by it.
entries.9:14: Paul says the Lord himself ordered that those who preach the good news should earn their living from it. For the reader, it means supporting those who share the gospel is something Jesus himself intended.
entries.9:15: Paul says he has not used any of these rights and is not writing to get support now, because he would rather die than lose this point of pride. For the reader, it means sometimes people choose to serve without payment to keep their motives pure.
entries.9:16: Paul says preaching the good news gives him no reason to boast, because he is compelled to do it and would be in trouble if he didn't. For the reader, it means when God calls you to something, you do it out of necessity, not for credit.
entries.9:17: Paul says that if he preaches willingly he gets a reward, but either way he is still under orders to do it. For the reader, it means obedience to God's calling is required, but doing it gladly brings its own reward.
entries.9:18: Paul says his reward is that he can preach the good news free of charge and not use his rights as a preacher. For the reader, it means true reward can come from serving generously rather than demanding what you are owed.
entries.9:19: Paul says that although he is free from everyone, he made himself a servant to all so that more people could be saved. For the reader, it means giving up your own freedom to serve others can help them come to faith.
entries.9:20: Paul says he became like a Jew to win Jews and like one under the law to win those under the law, without actually being under it himself. For the reader, it means meeting people where they are helps you connect with them, as long as your own convictions stay intact.
entries.9:21: Paul says he became like one without the law to win those without the law, while still being under Christ's law, not lawless toward God. For the reader, it means you can adapt to people's culture without abandoning your loyalty to Christ.
entries.9:22: Paul says he became weak to the weak and all things to all people so that some might be saved. For the reader, it means putting yourself in others' shoes is a way to help them find salvation.
entries.9:23: Paul says he does all this for the sake of the good news so that he can share in its blessings. For the reader, it means everything you do for the gospel is worth it because you share in its reward.
entries.9:24: Paul compares the Christian life to a race where many run but only one wins the prize, and urges them to run to win. For the reader, it means take your faith seriously and aim wholeheartedly for the reward God offers.
entries.9:25: Paul says athletes exercise self-control to win a temporary crown, but believers do it for an eternal one. For the reader, it means disciplining yourself is worth it because the reward God gives lasts forever.
entries.9:26: Paul says he runs with a clear goal and fights like someone who actually lands his punches, not swinging at air. For the reader, it means live your faith with purpose and direction, not aimlessly.
entries.9:27: Paul says he disciplines his body and keeps it under control so that after preaching to others he himself would not be disqualified. For the reader, it means take your own spiritual life seriously, not just helping others while neglecting yourself.
entries.10:1: Paul reminds the Corinthians that Israel's whole people had God's guidance and rescue, just as they did. It means we should remember God's past faithfulness and not assume we're different from those who failed.
entries.10:2: Israel was united to Moses when they passed through the sea under the cloud, a kind of baptism. It means God's people are joined together through his saving acts, not through their own merit.
entries.10:3: All the Israelites ate the same food God gave them in the desert. It means God provides for his people equally, but receiving his gifts is not the same as being faithful to him.
entries.10:4: They all drank water God provided from a rock, and Paul says that rock was Christ. It means Christ was already caring for God's people long before he came, so we should trust him as our source of life.
entries.10:5: Even though God blessed them, most of that generation displeased him and died in the desert. It means God's gifts don't excuse disobedience, and we should take warning.
entries.10:6: These events were written down as examples for us. It means we should learn from Israel's failures and not let our hearts chase evil things.
entries.10:7: Some Israelites turned to idols and then to wild partying. It means chasing false gods leads to selfish pleasure, and we should not follow that pattern.
entries.10:8: Some Israelites gave in to sexual sin and thousands died in one day. It means giving in to bodily desires can bring serious consequences, so we should take it seriously.
entries.10:9: Some Israelites tested the Lord and were killed by snakes. It means we should not push God's patience by demanding he prove himself or by grumbling against him.
entries.10:10: Some Israelites complained against God and were destroyed. It means grumbling and speaking against God is dangerous, so we should watch our words.
entries.10:11: These things happened and were recorded to teach people living in the final era. It means the Bible's old stories are practical warnings for us today, not just history.
entries.10:12: Anyone who feels secure should be careful not to fall. It means confidence in ourselves is risky, so we should stay humble and watchful.
entries.10:13: Every temptation comes with a way out, because God is faithful. You are not trapped; look for the exit.
entries.10:14: Because of these warnings, Paul tells his dear friends to stay away from idol worship. It means we should flee anything that takes God's rightful place in our lives.
entries.10:15: Paul asks sensible people to judge for themselves whether what he says makes sense. It means we should think carefully about his teaching rather than accept or reject it carelessly.
entries.10:16: The cup and bread of the Lord's Supper connect believers with Christ's blood and body. It means sharing communion is real fellowship with Christ, not just a ritual.
entries.10:17: Though many people, we are one bread and one body because we all share the one bread. It means communion should unite us as one community, not leave us isolated.
entries.10:18: Israelites who ate altar offerings were sharing in the altar itself. It means eating at a sacrifice joins you to what it represents, which matters for how we treat idol feasts.
entries.10:19: Paul clarifies that an idol is nothing and food offered to it is nothing in itself. It means the danger isn't in the object but in what the worship behind it involves.
entries.10:20: What pagans sacrifice, they offer to evil spirits, not to God, and Paul doesn't want believers joined to those spirits. It means idol worship is really partnership with dark powers, so we should avoid it.
entries.10:21: You can't drink from the Lord's cup and the cup of evil spirits at the same time. It means we can't split our loyalty between Christ and things that oppose him.
entries.10:22: Paul asks whether we want to make the Lord jealous and whether we think we're stronger than he is. It means provoking God is foolish, because we are not his equal.
entries.10:23: Believers are free to do many things, but not everything is helpful or builds others up. It means freedom should be guided by wisdom and concern for the common good.
entries.10:24: Each person should look out for others' good, not just their own. It means love means setting aside personal advantage for the sake of your neighbor.
entries.10:25: Buy and eat whatever meat is sold in the market without asking where it came from. It means don't be anxious about every detail; God's creation is good to receive.
entries.10:26: The whole earth belongs to the Lord and everything in it. It means no food is off-limits in itself, so we can receive it with thanks.
entries.10:27: If an unbeliever invites you to dinner, go and eat whatever is served without raising questions. It means be a gracious guest and don't turn ordinary meals into debates.
entries.10:28: But if someone tells you the food was offered to an idol, don't eat it for the sake of that person's conscience. It means love sometimes limits our freedom to protect someone else's convictions.
entries.10:29: Paul says the concern is the other person's conscience, not your own freedom. It means your rights don't cancel your responsibility to care how your actions affect others.
entries.10:30: If you thank God for your food, no one should criticize you for eating it. It means gratitude to God matters more than others' opinions about what you eat.
entries.10:31: Whatever you do, whether eating, drinking, or anything else, do it for God's glory. It means even ordinary daily choices should honor God.
entries.10:32: Don't cause trouble for Jews, Greeks, or the church of God. It means live in a way that doesn't trip up outsiders or fellow believers.
entries.10:33: Paul gives up his own advantage to seek others' good so they can be saved. It means putting others first is a pattern worth following, especially for their spiritual good.
entries.11:1: Paul tells the Corinthians to copy his way of living because he copies Christ. For you, it means looking at how faithful believers live as a pattern for following Jesus.
entries.11:2: Paul praises them for remembering him and holding on to the teachings he passed on. It means valuing and keeping the instruction you've received about following Jesus.
entries.11:3: Paul says God is over Christ, Christ is over every man, and the man is over the woman in God's order. It means God has a structure of authority, and each person relates to him within it.
entries.11:4: A man who prays or speaks God's message with his head covered brings shame on himself. In that culture, covering signaled something improper for a man leading in worship.
entries.11:5: A woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered shames herself, as if her hair were cut off. It means how we present ourselves in worship matters in that setting.
entries.11:6: If a woman won't cover her head, she might as well cut her hair; but since that's shameful, she should cover it. Paul is arguing from their own sense of honor and shame.
entries.11:7: A man shouldn't cover his head because he reflects God's image and glory, while the woman reflects the man's glory. It's about honor and order in worship, not about worth.
entries.11:8: Paul points back to creation: the man wasn't made from the woman, but the woman from the man. He's grounding his point about order in the creation account.
entries.11:9: The man wasn't created for the woman's sake, but the woman for the man's. Paul is describing God's design in creation, not saying women matter less.
entries.11:10: Because of this, and because of the angels, a woman should wear a sign of authority on her head. It means honoring God's order in worship, with angels as witnesses.
entries.11:11: Yet in the Lord, women and men are not independent of each other. It means neither sex can dismiss the other; they belong together in Christ.
entries.11:12: Just as the woman came from the man, so men are born through women, and everything comes from God. It means men and women depend on each other under God.
entries.11:13: Paul asks them to judge for themselves whether it seems proper for a woman to pray uncovered. He's appealing to their sense of what's fitting in worship.
entries.11:14: Paul appeals to what seems natural to them: long hair on a man is a disgrace in their culture. It's about what their society considered honorable.
entries.11:15: Long hair on a woman is her glory, and her hair is given as a covering. Paul uses their natural sense of honor to support his point about covering.
entries.11:16: If anyone wants to argue about this, neither we nor God's churches have any other practice. It means this was the settled custom, not something to fight over.
entries.11:17: Paul says their meetings were doing more harm than good. It means gathering as a church can go wrong if hearts and behavior aren't right.
entries.11:18: Paul heard there were divisions when they met, and he partly believes it. It means disunity in a church is a serious problem worth addressing.
entries.11:19: Divisions are bound to happen so that those who are genuine become clear. It means conflict can reveal who is truly faithful.
entries.11:20: Because of their behavior, their gathering couldn't really be the Lord's Supper. It means wrong attitudes can ruin a sacred meal.
entries.11:21: Each person ate their own meal first, so one went hungry and another got drunk. It means selfishness turned a shared meal into a disgrace.
entries.11:22: Paul asks if they have no homes to eat in, and accuses them of shaming the poor and the church. It means treating others badly at church is unacceptable.
entries.11:23: Paul passes on what he received from the Lord: on the night Jesus was betrayed, he took bread. It means this teaching about the meal comes from Jesus himself.
entries.11:24: After giving thanks, Jesus said the bread was his body given for them, and told them to do this in memory of him. It means the meal is a way to remember his sacrifice.
entries.11:25: After the meal, Jesus took the cup and said it was the new covenant in his blood, to be done in memory of him. It means his death established a new relationship with God.
entries.11:26: Every time you eat the bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he returns. It means the meal declares what Jesus did and looks forward to his coming.
entries.11:27: Anyone who takes the bread or cup in a wrong spirit is guilty concerning the Lord's body and blood. It means treating this meal carelessly is a serious matter.
entries.11:28: Each person should examine themselves before eating the bread and drinking the cup. It means checking your own heart and attitude before coming to the table.
entries.11:29: A person who eats and drinks without recognizing the Lord's body brings judgment on themselves. It means not taking the meal seriously has real consequences.
entries.11:30: Because of this, many among them were weak and sick, and some had died. Paul sees their careless behavior as having serious results.
entries.11:31: If we judged ourselves honestly, we wouldn't come under judgment. It means self-examination spares us from discipline.
entries.11:32: When the Lord judges us, it's discipline to keep us from being condemned with the world. It means God corrects his people out of love, not to destroy them.
entries.11:33: When you gather for the Lord's meal, wait for one another. It means putting others first so everyone can share together.
entries.11:34: If anyone is hungry, they should eat at home so the gathering doesn't bring judgment. It means keeping the church meal distinct and orderly, and Paul will settle the rest later.
entries.12:1: Paul doesn't want these believers to be confused or uninformed about spiritual gifts. He's saying that understanding how God's Spirit works matters for everyday life.
entries.12:2: Before they knew God, they were led along by lifeless idols that couldn't speak or help. Paul reminds them of that past so they can see how different life in the Spirit is.
entries.12:3: The real test of whether something comes from God's Spirit is what it says about Jesus. Anyone truly speaking by the Spirit will honor Jesus as Lord, not curse him.
entries.12:4: God gives a variety of gifts, but they all come from the same Spirit. Differences in ability don't mean different sources.
entries.12:5: There are many kinds of service, yet all of it is for the same Lord. The variety doesn't change who we're serving.
entries.12:6: God works in many different ways, but it's the same God doing the work in everyone. No one's role is outside his activity.
entries.12:7: Every believer gets some way the Spirit works through them, and it's given to benefit everyone, not just the person who has it.
entries.12:8: The Spirit gives one person insight to speak wisely and another person solid understanding of truth. Both come from the same source.
entries.12:9: To one person the Spirit gives strong trust in God, and to another the ability to heal the sick. Both are gifts from the one Spirit.
entries.12:10: The Spirit gives various abilities: doing powerful works, speaking God's message, telling true spirits from false, speaking in other languages, and explaining what those languages mean.
entries.12:11: All these gifts come from the same Spirit, who decides what each person receives. No one earns or controls them.
entries.12:12: A human body is one thing made of many parts, and that's a picture of Christ's people. Many members, but one body.
entries.12:13: Through the one Spirit we were all brought into one body, whatever our background or status, and we all share the same Spirit.
entries.12:14: A body isn't just a single part; it's made up of many parts. That's how God designed it.
entries.12:15: A foot that feels inferior because it isn't a hand is still genuinely part of the body. Feeling less important doesn't make you less included.
entries.12:16: An ear that wishes it were an eye is still part of the body. Comparing yourself to others doesn't change your place.
entries.12:17: If the whole body were just one part, it couldn't do all the things a body needs to do. Different parts are necessary.
entries.12:18: God himself placed each part in the body just as he wanted. Your place isn't an accident.
entries.12:19: If everything were the same single part, there would be no body at all. Variety is what makes a body work.
entries.12:20: The reality is many different parts forming one body. Difference and unity go together.
entries.12:21: No part can tell another part it isn't needed. Everyone's contribution matters, even if it looks less prominent.
entries.12:22: The parts that seem weakest are often the most necessary. Don't dismiss what looks unimportant.
entries.12:23: We give extra care and respect to the parts of the body that seem less honorable. Treating the overlooked with dignity reflects how God builds his people.
entries.12:24: The presentable parts don't need special attention, so God arranged the body to give honor to the parts that lack it. He balances things so no one is left out.
entries.12:25: God's aim is that the body stays unified, with every part caring for the others equally. Division among believers works against his design.
entries.12:26: When one part suffers, the whole body feels it, and when one part is honored, all share the joy. We're meant to feel each other's pain and celebrate each other's good.
entries.12:27: Together you are Christ's body, and each of you is a distinct part of it. You belong, and you have a role.
entries.12:28: God set different roles in the church, from apostles and prophets to teachers, miracle workers, healers, helpers, and those who guide or speak in other languages. Not everyone has the same job.
entries.12:29: Not everyone is an apostle, prophet, or teacher, and not everyone works miracles. Different gifts are given to different people.
entries.12:30: Not everyone heals, speaks in tongues, or explains them. The questions expect a no, showing that gifts vary by God's design.
entries.12:31: Paul tells them to eagerly desire the greater gifts, then announces he'll show them a way that's even better than any gift.
entries.13:1: Even if you could speak in every language, human or angelic, without love it is just empty noise. Your impressive abilities mean nothing to others if you don't actually care about them.
entries.13:2: You could have deep insight, secret knowledge, and faith that moves mountains, but without love you are worth nothing. What you know and believe matters less than whether you love.
entries.13:3: You could give away everything you own or even sacrifice your own body, but if love isn't behind it, it does you no good. Generous or heroic acts done without love don't count for much.
entries.13:4: Love is patient and kind, and it doesn't get jealous or boast or act proud. This is the everyday test of whether what you're doing is really love.
entries.13:5: Love doesn't act rudely, doesn't put itself first, doesn't fly off the handle, and doesn't keep a record of wrongs. Real love lets go of grudges and thinks of others.
entries.13:6: Love doesn't enjoy it when wrong things happen but is glad when the truth wins. Love sides with what is right and honest.
entries.13:7: Love puts up with a lot, keeps trusting, keeps hoping, and doesn't give up. Love hangs in there even when things are hard.
entries.13:8: Prophecy, tongues, and knowledge will all fade away, but love never ends. Whatever else you build your life on, love is the one thing that lasts.
entries.13:9: Our knowledge and our prophetic insight are only partial right now. We don't see or understand everything, and that's okay.
entries.13:10: When the complete thing arrives, the partial things will no longer be needed. One day what is incomplete in us will be finished.
entries.13:11: When you were a child you talked, thought, and reasoned like a child, but growing up means leaving childish ways behind. Growing in love is part of becoming mature.
entries.13:12: Right now we see things dimly, like looking into a cloudy mirror, but one day we will see clearly and know fully. You don't have the whole picture yet, and that's expected.
entries.13:13: Faith, hope, and love remain, and love is the greatest of the three. Of everything you can pursue, love is the most important.
entries.14:1: Paul tells the Corinthians to make love their top priority and to eagerly want spiritual gifts, especially the ability to speak God's message to others. Readers should pursue love first and desire gifts that build others up.
entries.14:2: Someone speaking in a tongue is speaking to God, not to people, since no one present understands what is said—it is a mystery spoken by the Spirit. This means such speech can be real worship even when others gain nothing from it.
entries.14:3: When someone speaks God's message, it helps people understand, encourages them, and strengthens them. The test of a message is whether it builds others up.
entries.14:4: Speaking in a tongue may benefit the speaker personally, but speaking God's message benefits the whole church. Readers should value what helps the community, not just themselves.
entries.14:5: Paul wishes everyone could speak in tongues, but he would rather they speak God's message, since that helps the church unless tongues are interpreted. The greater good is what builds others up.
entries.14:6: If Paul came speaking in tongues, it would do the Corinthians no good unless he also brought them understanding, a message from God, or teaching. Helpful communication requires content others can grasp.
entries.14:7: Like a flute or harp, if an instrument makes no distinct notes, no one can tell what tune is being played. Speech that no one can understand communicates nothing.
entries.14:8: If a battle trumpet gives an unclear sound, no one knows to prepare for war. Unclear speech fails to move people to action.
entries.14:9: If you speak in a tongue with no understandable words, you are just talking into the air—no one can grasp what you say. Readers should speak so others can understand.
entries.14:10: There are many languages in the world, and each one carries meaning. Every language matters, but meaning depends on someone understanding it.
entries.14:11: If I don't understand the language being spoken, the speaker and I are like foreigners to each other. Understanding is what makes communication work.
entries.14:12: Since you eagerly want spiritual gifts, aim first for those that build up the church. Desire should be directed toward helping others.
entries.14:13: Anyone who speaks in a tongue should pray for the ability to interpret it. That way the gift can benefit others, not just the speaker.
entries.14:14: If I pray in a tongue, my spirit is praying but my mind is not engaged. Paul wants prayer that involves understanding too.
entries.14:15: So pray with both spirit and mind, and sing with both spirit and mind. Worship should engage your understanding, not bypass it.
entries.14:16: If you bless God in a tongue, an outsider can't say amen because he doesn't know what you said. Worship should be understandable enough for others to join in.
entries.14:17: Your thanksgiving may be fine in itself, but it does nothing to help the person who doesn't understand. Good intentions don't replace clear communication.
entries.14:18: Paul thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than any of them. He is not against the gift—he simply wants it used well.
entries.14:19: In church, five understandable words that teach others are better than ten thousand words in a tongue. What helps people understand is worth more than impressive but unclear speech.
entries.14:20: Don't be childish in your thinking; be innocent about evil but mature in understanding. Grow up in how you think about these matters.
entries.14:21: God says through the law that he will speak to his people through foreign languages, yet even then they won't listen. Tongues can serve as a sign, but they don't guarantee a response.
entries.14:22: Tongues are a sign aimed at unbelievers, while God's message is meant for those who believe. Each gift has its purpose and audience.
entries.14:23: If the whole church speaks in tongues and outsiders come in, they will think you are out of your minds. Unclear worship can confuse and repel visitors.
entries.14:24: But if everyone speaks God's message and an outsider comes in, he is confronted and examined by what everyone says. Clear prophetic speech can reach an unbeliever's heart.
entries.14:25: The secrets of his heart are exposed, and he falls down and worships God, declaring that God is truly among you. Understandable words can lead someone to faith.
entries.14:26: When you gather, each person may bring a song, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation—but everything should be done to build others up. Every contribution should serve the common good.
entries.14:27: If tongues are spoken, limit it to two or three people, one at a time, and someone must interpret. Order and understanding keep the gift from causing confusion.
entries.14:28: If no interpreter is present, the tongue-speaker should stay silent in the meeting and speak only to himself and God. Not every gift needs to be displayed publicly.
entries.14:29: Two or three prophets may speak, and the others should weigh what is said. Messages should be tested, not just accepted.
entries.14:30: If someone sitting nearby receives a revelation, the first speaker should stop. There is room for others to share, and no one should monopolize the meeting.
entries.14:31: You can all speak God's message one at a time so everyone can learn and be encouraged. Taking turns lets the whole group benefit.
entries.14:32: Prophets can control their own spirits. Being moved by the Spirit does not mean losing self-control or disrupting the meeting.
entries.14:33: God is not a God of disorder but of peace, as in all the churches. Worship should reflect his character by being peaceful and orderly.
entries.14:34: Paul says women should be quiet in the churches and not speak there, but remain under control, as the law says. He is addressing disorder in that setting, and readers should take his instruction seriously while comparing it with the rest of Scripture.
entries.14:35: If women want to learn something, they should ask their husbands at home, because speaking in the church brings shame. Paul directs their questions to a private setting rather than public disruption.
entries.14:36: Paul challenges the Corinthians: did God's word originate with you, or are you the only ones it reached? No church gets to set its own rules apart from God's word.
entries.14:37: Anyone who claims to be a prophet or spiritual should recognize that what Paul writes is the Lord's command. Claims to spiritual authority must submit to God's word.
entries.14:38: If anyone ignores this, let him be ignored. Those who refuse God's instruction are not to be catered to.
entries.14:39: So eagerly desire to speak God's message, and don't forbid speaking in tongues. Both gifts matter, but prophecy is to be especially sought.
entries.14:40: Everything should be done properly and in order. Good worship is both sincere and well-ordered.
entries.15:1: Paul is reminding the Corinthians of the message he first preached to them, which they accepted and built their faith on. It means the good news they received is the foundation they should keep standing on.
entries.15:2: This same message is what saves them, but only if they hold firmly to it and their faith actually does something. It means salvation is tied to staying committed to what they were taught, not just hearing it once.
entries.15:3: Paul passed on the most important thing he himself had received: that Christ died for our sins, which the Scriptures had already foretold. It means the heart of the faith is that Jesus' death dealt with our wrongdoing.
entries.15:4: He was buried, and then on the third day he rose from the dead, just as the Scriptures said. It means the resurrection is a real event that was predicted beforehand, not an afterthought.
entries.15:5: After rising, Jesus appeared to Peter and then to the group of twelve disciples. It means real people actually saw the risen Jesus, which is the evidence the message rests on.
entries.15:6: He also appeared to more than five hundred believers at once, most of whom were still alive when Paul wrote this. It means there were plenty of living witnesses who could be checked, so the claim wasn't based on rumor.
entries.15:7: He then appeared to James and afterward to all the apostles. It means the resurrection was confirmed to the leaders of the church as well, not just to a few.
entries.15:8: Last of all, Jesus appeared to Paul too, though he compares himself to a baby born at the wrong time. It means Paul knew he was an unusual, late addition to the witnesses.
entries.15:9: Paul says he is the least of the apostles and doesn't even deserve the title, because he had violently persecuted God's church. It means his past was genuinely bad, and he wasn't pretending otherwise.
entries.15:10: But God's undeserved kindness made him what he is, and that kindness wasn't wasted, since he worked harder than all the others, though really it was God's grace working through him. It means God can turn even a guilty past into something useful.
entries.15:11: Whether it was Paul or the other apostles preaching, they all preached the same message, and that is what the Corinthians believed. It means the core message is the same no matter who tells it.
entries.15:12: Since the good news says Christ rose from the dead, Paul asks how some of them can claim there is no resurrection at all. It means their belief contradicts the very message they accepted.
entries.15:13: If dead people don't rise, then Christ didn't rise either. It means you can't deny resurrection in general and still keep Christ's resurrection.
entries.15:14: And if Christ didn't rise, then the preaching is empty and so is their faith. It means everything they believe stands or falls on the resurrection.
entries.15:15: Worse, the apostles would be caught lying about God, since they claimed he raised Christ, which wouldn't be true if the dead don't rise. It means denying the resurrection makes the preachers false witnesses.
entries.15:16: Paul repeats the point: if the dead can't be raised, then Christ wasn't raised. It means the logic is unavoidable.
entries.15:17: And if Christ wasn't raised, their faith is useless and they are still guilty of their sins. It means without the resurrection, forgiveness and salvation don't actually happen.
entries.15:18: Also, those who died believing in Christ would have simply perished. It means denying the resurrection would mean the faithful dead are lost for good.
entries.15:19: If our hope in Christ only counts for this life, we are the most pitiful people of all. It means the Christian hope has to reach beyond death, or it's not worth much.
entries.15:20: But the truth is Christ really has risen, the first of all who have died to be raised. It means his resurrection guarantees that others will be raised too.
entries.15:21: Death came through one man, and resurrection from the dead also comes through one man. It means Jesus reverses the damage that started with Adam.
entries.15:22: Just as everyone dies because of Adam, so everyone who belongs to Christ will be made alive. It means Christ brings life to all who are his, just as Adam brought death to all.
entries.15:23: But each in the proper order: Christ first, then those who belong to him when he returns. It means the resurrection happens in stages, not all at once.
entries.15:24: After that comes the end, when Christ hands the kingdom over to God the Father, having destroyed every rival rule and authority and power. It means Christ's work finishes with all opposition gone and God fully in charge.
entries.15:25: Christ must keep ruling until he has put all his enemies under his feet. It means his reign continues until every enemy is defeated.
entries.15:26: The very last enemy to be destroyed is death itself. It means death, the final foe, will not last forever.
entries.15:27: Scripture says God put everything under Christ's feet, though obviously that doesn't include God himself, who did the putting. It means Christ's authority is total, but under God's authority.
entries.15:28: When everything is under Christ, the Son himself will be under God, who put all things under him, so that God may be everything to everyone. It means the goal of it all is God fully ruling over a restored creation.
entries.15:29: Paul asks what people are doing getting baptized on behalf of the dead, if the dead aren't raised at all. It means their own practice makes no sense if there's no resurrection.
entries.15:30: And why would the apostles put themselves in danger every hour? It means risking your life only makes sense if there's life after death.
entries.15:31: Paul says he faces death daily, and he swears by the pride he has in them in Christ Jesus. It means his constant danger proves he believes in something beyond this life.
entries.15:32: If he fought wild beasts at Ephesus for merely human reasons, what did he gain? If the dead don't rise, we might as well eat and drink, since tomorrow we die. It means without resurrection, self-sacrifice is pointless and pleasure is all that's left.
entries.15:33: Don't be fooled: bad company ruins good character. It means the people you spend time with will shape how you live.
entries.15:34: Wake up and live rightly, and stop sinning, because some of you don't really know God, and Paul says this to shame them. It means wrong beliefs about resurrection were leading to careless living.
entries.15:35: Someone might ask how the dead are raised and what kind of body they will have. It means people naturally wonder about the details of resurrection.
entries.15:36: Paul calls that a foolish question, and points out that a seed has to die in the ground before it can come to life. It means death is the necessary step before new life, just like a seed.
entries.15:37: When you plant a seed, you don't plant the full plant that will grow, just the bare seed. It means the body we have now is not the same as the body we will have.
entries.15:38: But God gives it a body as he chooses, and each kind of seed gets its own body. It means God decides what the resurrection body will be like, and it fits each person.
entries.15:39: Not all flesh is the same: people, animals, birds, and fish each have their own kind. It means different kinds of bodies exist, so a resurrection body can be different from our current one.
entries.15:40: There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, and their splendor differs. It means the glory of the resurrection body will be different from and greater than our present bodies.
entries.15:41: Just as the sun, moon, and stars each shine with their own kind of brightness, risen bodies will differ in splendor. Your future glory will be real and distinct, not a dull copy of someone else's.
entries.15:42: The resurrection works like planting a seed: the body we bury is dead, but what comes up is alive. Death is not the end of you; it is the beginning of a new kind of life.
entries.15:43: The body we bury looks weak and shameful, but the body raised will be glorious and strong. Your present weakness and humiliation will not last; God will replace them with honor and power.
entries.15:44: What is buried is an ordinary physical body, but what is raised is a body suited to the spirit. Since there is a physical body, God also has a spiritual body waiting for you.
entries.15:45: Adam received life as a living being, but Christ, the last Adam, gives life to others. Jesus does not just live; he shares his life with you.
entries.15:46: The physical comes first and the spiritual comes afterward. You should not expect spiritual fullness now; God's pattern is ordinary life first, then the life of the Spirit.
entries.15:47: The first man came from dust, while the second man, Christ, comes from heaven. Your origin is dust, but your future is tied to the one from heaven.
entries.15:48: People made of dust resemble Adam, and people of heaven resemble Christ. You will become like the one you belong to, so your hope is to share Christ's heavenly likeness.
entries.15:49: Just as you now bear the likeness of the earthly Adam, you will one day bear the likeness of the heavenly Christ. Your current earthly nature is not your final form.
entries.15:50: Ordinary flesh and blood cannot inherit God's kingdom, and perishable things cannot share in what never dies. You need a changed body, not just a patched-up old one.
entries.15:51: Paul reveals a secret: not every believer will die, but every believer will be transformed. Death is not guaranteed for you, but change is.
entries.15:52: This change will happen instantly, in a flash, when the last trumpet sounds. The dead will be raised never to die again, and those still alive will be changed too.
entries.15:53: Our decaying bodies must be freed from death and clothed with what lasts forever. What is mortal in you will be swallowed up by life.
entries.15:54: When that change happens, the old prophecy comes true: death is defeated by life. Death's grip on you will be broken for good.
entries.15:55: Death is taunted as powerless, its sting gone. The enemy that once seemed unbeatable will have nothing left to threaten you with.
entries.15:56: Sin is what makes death painful, and the law is what gives sin its force. Christ has dealt with both, so death's sting is removed.
entries.15:57: The win over death is given to you, not earned by you. Thank God rather than yourself.
entries.15:58: Because of this sure hope, stand firm and keep working for the Lord. Nothing you do for him is wasted, even when you cannot see the results.
entries.16:1: Paul tells the Corinthians to collect money for needy believers, just as he told the churches in Galatia to do. Giving to help other Christians is a normal part of church life, not an optional extra.
entries.16:2: Each week, on the first day, every person should set aside some money in proportion to what they earned. This means planning your giving regularly instead of scrambling to collect it at the last minute.
entries.16:3: When Paul arrives, he will send trusted men chosen by the church to carry the collected money to Jerusalem. The church decides who handles the money, and it is delivered with letters of explanation.
entries.16:4: If it makes sense for Paul to go to Jerusalem too, these chosen men will travel with him. He is flexible about the details but committed to getting the gift delivered.
entries.16:5: Paul plans to travel through Macedonia first and then come to Corinth. He is telling them his travel plans so they know what to expect.
entries.16:6: He may stay with them for a while, perhaps through the winter, and then they can help him on his way. A longer visit would let them build a real relationship rather than a quick hello.
entries.16:7: Paul doesn't want just a brief stopover on his way somewhere else; he hopes to spend real time with them if the Lord allows. Plans should always be made with God's will in mind.
entries.16:8: Paul will stay in Ephesus until the festival of Pentecost. He is explaining his current schedule so they understand why he isn't coming right away.
entries.16:9: Ephesus offers a wide-open opportunity for effective work, but there are also many people opposing him. Big opportunities often come with big opposition, and that doesn't mean you're doing something wrong.
entries.16:10: If Timothy visits, treat him kindly and make him feel safe, because he is doing the Lord's work just as Paul is. Don't intimidate or look down on younger workers for God.
entries.16:11: Respect Timothy properly and help him leave in peace so he can return to Paul, who is waiting for him along with the other brothers. Support the people who serve God rather than making things hard for them.
entries.16:12: Paul really wanted Apollos to visit with the brothers, but Apollos chose not to come now; he will come when he gets a chance. Even good leaders make their own decisions, and that's fine.
entries.16:13: Stay alert, hold firmly to the faith, and be courageous and strong. The Christian life requires watchfulness and strength, not passive drifting.
entries.16:14: Whatever you do, do it with love. Love should be the motive behind every action, including all the instructions Paul has just given.
entries.16:15: The household of Stephanas were the first believers in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to serving other believers. You probably know people like this, and Paul wants the church to recognize them.
entries.16:16: Submit to leaders like these and to everyone who works hard alongside them in the Lord's work. Give proper respect to those who serve faithfully.
entries.16:17: Paul is glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus came, because they supplied what the Corinthians couldn't. Their visit filled a gap and encouraged Paul.
entries.16:18: These men refreshed Paul's spirit and the Corinthians' too, so give people like them proper respect. Recognize and honor those who bring comfort and encouragement.
entries.16:19: The churches in Asia send their greetings, and so do Aquila and Prisca along with the church that meets in their home. Believers are connected across distances, and house churches were a normal part of early Christian life.
entries.16:20: All the brothers send greetings, and Paul tells them to greet one another with a holy kiss. A warm, appropriate greeting shows real family affection among believers.
entries.16:21: Paul writes this greeting in his own handwriting, which shows the letter is genuinely from him. A personal touch matters, even in a formal letter.
entries.16:22: Anyone who does not love the Lord is under judgment, and Paul adds the Aramaic prayer 'Our Lord, come!' Loving Jesus is essential, and we should long for his return.
entries.16:23: Paul prays that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ will be with them. Grace, God's undeserved kindness, is the foundation of everything.
entries.16:24: Paul ends by saying his love is with all of them in Christ Jesus. Even after correcting them sharply, he wants them to know he genuinely loves them.
